Raising immediately turns a subtle correctness bug into a fast, obvious, fixable one. *Advanced:* "Walk me through exactly why *not* rescaling to [0,1] matters here." — EfficientNet's Keras implementation includes its own internal Rescaling/normalization layer at the front of the network, calibrated to expect raw [0, 255] pixel values.

Evaluation used to resize with Keras load_img (nearest-neighbour, as in the published notebooks) while both serving paths resize with PIL's default (bicubic), so the previous model's reported 91.25% described a computation nobody was served; measured on the serving path it scores 90.25%.
Input: 256×256×3 RGB, raw [0,255] pixels (EfficientNet applies its own rescaling internally — do not divide by 255).

This is a specific, actionable, non-obvious result — it tells a reader exactly which real-world failure mode (sensor/scanner noise) this particular model needs the most protection against, information a single averaged "68.3% mean corrupted accuracy" number would completely hide.

Training (btc/finetune.py, 21.5 min on an Apple M3 Pro CPU, seed 75): 1. head only on cached features of the frozen ImageNet backbone (each image and its mirror), Adamax 1e-3, early-stopped on validation accuracy; 2. fine-tune from block6a up with flips, small rotations/zooms/shifts, brightness/contrast and Gaussian noise, Adamax 1e-4 reduced on validation plateaus, BatchNorm frozen throughout.
